name: Dimethicone
lead: Dimethicone, also known as polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) or dimethylpolysiloxane, is a silicone polymer and a type of silicone oil. It ranges from a pourable liquid to a rubbery semi-solid depending on chain length, and it is hydrophobic and optically clear.[1]

In skin and hair products it is widely used as a skin-protectant and conditioning ingredient, listed in moisturizing lotions and sometimes present at concentrations up to about 15 percent, and in shampoos and conditioners to add slip and shine.[1] The Cosmetic Ingredient Review Expert Panel has concluded that dimethicone and related polymers are safe as used in cosmetic formulations.[1]

Published human studies of dimethicone concern medical uses such as incontinence-associated dermatitis and head lice rather than appearance outcomes. Consumers mainly encounter it as an ingredient in moisturizers and hair products, and product labels list it as a skin protectant.[2]

paras: Dimethicone has the formula CH3[Si(CH3)2O]nSi(CH3)3, with chains capped by trimethylsilyl groups. Commercial material is made by base-catalysed ring-opening polymerisation of cyclic siloxanes. Viscosity rises with chain length, from a thin oil to a rubbery semi-solid.[1]
It is hydrophobic and is not appreciably swollen by water or alcohols, although many organic solvents swell it.[1]

Dimethicone is common in moisturizing lotions, often listed for skin protection, and is described as feeling lighter than typical plant or mineral oils.[1] In hair care it adds shine and slipperiness to shampoos and conditioners; an amino-modified relative, amodimethicone, is described as a more effective conditioner for damaged hair.[1] Dimethicone/methicone copolymer is also used as a coating on nano-sized titanium dioxide particles in sunscreens.[4]

Activated dimethicone (simethicone) is used as an antifoaming agent in over-the-counter medicines and in food, and dimethicone is used as a head-lice treatment, thought to act by blocking water excretion rather than by suffocation.[1] It also appears in condom lubricants, sealants and silicone greases.[1]

Trials involving dimethicone have mostly examined medical rather than cosmetic outcomes. A randomised controlled trial compared a perineal care washcloth impregnated with 3 percent dimethicone against water and pH-neutral soap for preventing and treating incontinence-associated dermatitis.[5] Registered trials have compared a 4 percent dimethicone foam with permethrin cream rinse for head lice[6] and have used dimethicone-containing agents in endoscopy preparation.[7] No published trial found in the sources examines dimethicone for improving facial appearance, skin texture or hair quality in healthy people.
A minipig study of sunscreens found no significant dermal penetration of titanium dioxide particles, including dimethicone/methicone copolymer-coated nano-particles.[4]

The Cosmetic Ingredient Review Expert Panel concluded that dimethicone and related polymers are safe as used in cosmetic formulations, and the European Food Safety Authority's 2020 re-evaluation of E 900 found no safety concerns for reported food uses while recommending a limit on residual cyclic siloxanes from manufacturing.[1]
Silicone granuloma of facial tissues has been described in case reports following injection of liquid silicone, which is a different route and use from topical dimethicone.[8]

Referencing an industrial chemistry encyclopedia, Wikipedia notes that no marked harmful effects on organisms have been recorded for siloxanes; PDMS is not biodegradable but is captured in wastewater treatment.[1]

card.summary: A silicone oil used as a skin protectant and hair-smoothing ingredient; trials cover medical uses, not appearance outcomes.
card.note: Cosmetic safety panels rate it safe as used; liquid silicone injection is a separate, documented source of granulomas.

quick.overview:
Dimethicone is a silicone oil found in many moisturizers, primers, shampoos and conditioners. It gives a smooth, slippery feel and forms a water-repellent film on skin and hair.

Published human trials involve medical uses such as dermatitis and head lice; none were found testing it for improving appearance in healthy people.
quick.mechanism: It is a long-chain silicone polymer that is hydrophobic and leaves a thin protective layer on the surface of skin or hair, which accounts for its conditioning and smoothing effect.
quick.risks: The Cosmetic Ingredient Review panel concluded it is safe as used in cosmetics. Silicone granulomas reported in the literature arise from injected liquid silicone, not topical use. It is not biodegradable but is removed in wastewater treatment.
